Damon Rarick, Associate Professor Department of Modern and Classical Languages and Literatures College of Arts & Sciences Damon is starting his third term as Faculty Senator (2013–16, 2019–22, 2026-29) and has previously served on the Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC 2x); the Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC); the General Education Committee (GEC, chair); the Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC); the Subcommittee on the Assessment of General Education (SAGE); the Joint Committee for Academic Planning (JCAP); the Joint Committee for Online and Distance Learning (JCODL); the Faculty Senate Nominating Committee; the Faculty Senate Outstanding Service Award Committee; the Library Subcommittee on the 2020 URI Library; and the NEASC Comprehensive Evaluation Working Group.
He has also served on the A&S Scholastic Standing and Petitions Committee, the URI Foundation Excellence in Teaching Award Committee, and the Sabbatical Review Committee.
Beyond URI, Damon has held leadership positions in several national and regional organizations.

He served on the Executive Council of the American Association of Teachers of German (AATG), its Executive Steering Committee, External Investment Committee, Finance Committee, Membership Committee, and German for Professional Purposes Steering Committee; the national Käthe Wilson Scholarship Awards Committee (chair), and served as a voting delegate to the American Council on the Teaching of Foreign Languages.
He has served as president of the Rhode Island AATG and has served on the Advisory Board of the Rhode Island Foreign Language Association, the Editorial Board of Global Business Languages, and the Brown University Community Council.
He co-founded the Online Journal for Global Engineering Education and its successor, the Journal of International Engineering Education, which is now co-edited by our own Dr.
Sigrid Berka (URI) and Dr.
Brent Jesiek (Purdue).
Damon has been a recipient of the URI Foundation Excellence in Teaching Award and two of his courses received recognition in the Educational Policy Improvement Center’s AP Best Practices Course Study in World Languages, which guided AP exam development.

He has co-written a two-year textbook series called Impuls Deutsch that has been adopted by 150 colleges and high schools in the US market.
Candidate Statement I would like to boast that my work on committees spanning the curriculum, assessment, general education, academic planning, technologies, and accreditation has given me a keen ability to understand the inner workings and needs of the Faculty Senate and the University itself.
In reality, I simply enjoy working with bright, caring people across the University to ﬁnd creative, meaningful, sometimes elegant and often astoundingly effective solutions to problems facing this institution.
The connections we have between colleges, disciplines, and administrative units are both our strength and our guide.
They remind us of the importance of taking care of one another, working constructively across academic and institutional boundaries, and protecting shared governance, academic freedom, and advocacy itself during tumultuous times.
URI has weathered past transformational challenges, including the complete reform of the General Education Program, the global pandemic, and the ﬁrst years of the intensifying demographic cliff we are facing.

Uncertainty seems to be the word that best encapsulates the challenges we face today — challenges that affect the process of decision-making itself.
I do not have all the answers, but I have spent a long time learning how to ﬁnd them with others, and I would be honored to do that work on behalf of URI's faculty as a member of the Executive Committee or in any other capacity.

Laura Meyerson, Professor Natural Resources Science Having served on the URI faculty for over two decades, I bring deep institutional knowledge, commitment to shared governance, and a record of working across departments, colleges, and national and international organizations to advance the mission of higher education.
URI is navigating a period of significant institutional complexity, including a new budget model, changing federal priorities, pressures on research and teaching, and the continuing need to protect academic freedom, faculty voices, and transparent decision-making.
I would welcome the opportunity to help the Faculty Senate meet these challenges.
My previous Faculty Senate service (2019-22) gave me a broad understanding of Senate processes and responsibilities.
I served on the Curriculum Affairs Committee, chaired the University Calendar Committee, served on the Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC), and the Joint Committee on Academic Planning and the Academic Freedom Committee (JCAP).
These roles gave me practical experience in policy development, curriculum review, academic planning, faculty advocacy, and collaborative governance.

My Senate service was recognized through the URI President David and Reverend Lynn Dooley Faculty Senate Award for Important Contributions to the Faculty Senate and the Fritz Wenisch Award for Exceptional Contributions to the URI Faculty Senate.
Beyond Faculty Senate, my URI service has included chairing and serving on faculty search and review committees, serving on the Student Conduct Board, and directing programs in Environmental Science and Management and Restoration Science and Management.
My broader leadership experience includes serving as Editor-in-Chief of Biological Invasions , as a Coordinating Lead Author for the IPBES Invasive Alien Species Assessment, as a member of IUCN and national advisory groups, US National Invasive Species Council Invasive Species Science Advisory Board.
These experiences have trained me to listen carefully, synthesize complex information, build consensus, and move collective work forward.

If elected, I would bring that same level of commitment to the Executive Committee: a commitment to transparent governance, academic freedom, equity across disciplines, responsible curriculum processes, and strong faculty participation in decisions that shape URI’s future.
I would be honored to again serve the faculty in this leadership capacity.

GEC End-of-Year Report for the May 7, 2026, Faculty Senate Meeting
General Education Assessment: C2 and D1 Outcomes
This is a summary of the key findings and recommendations from the General Education assessment, focusing on the C2—Global Responsibilities—and D1—Integrate and Apply—outcomes.
Starting with C2: the expectation is that all students reach competency by graduation. The outcome is designed to position students within a global framework by asking them to engage with histories, cultures, institutions, and languages, and to move beyond understanding toward identifying and analyzing responsible action in response to complex global issues. In principle, it’s one of the most ambitious components of the GenEd program: it aims to cultivate knowledge and foster a sense of ethical responsibility and purpose within an interconnected world. Among the most urgent findings, which is echoed in both assessment data and anticipated student feedback, is the persistently low level of proficiency in a language other than English among our students. This isn’t a marginal issue; it represents a structural weakness in the current GenEd framework.

What we see in the data is partial progress toward that goal. Most students place at the level of approaching competency, with stronger performance in applying regional knowledge, understanding global systems, and reflecting on their own cultural perspective. These are important strengths that suggest our curriculum is building foundational global awareness effectively.
However, there are consistent gaps. Students struggle most with communicating in a language other than English, considering multiple perspectives, and—most notably—examining global responsibilities. Even at the upper levels, where we see developmental gains, these areas remain underdeveloped. The data suggest that students are better at knowing than at doing—that is, they can describe global issues but are less prepared to engage them critically or propose solutions.
We also note a structural limitation: only about 37% of courses participated in the C2 assessment. That level of participation constrains how broadly we can generalize these findings.

Turning to D1: this outcome is intended to move students beyond disciplinary silos by emphasizing the interconnectedness of knowledge and its application to complex, real-world problems. Positioned primarily at the 300- and 400-level, it assumes that students will draw on prior learning across the GenEd curriculum to synthesize ideas, transfer skills, and respond effectively to new academic and professional challenges. In this sense, D1 represents the culminating logic of GenEds: not just the accumulation of knowledge, but its integration and use.
Here the results are stronger. Students most often meet or approach competency, particularly in transferring skills, connecting knowledge, and engaging in integrative learning. This is encouraging and suggests that, where integration is explicitly built into coursework, students perform well.

That said, the D1 data come with even more significant limitations. Only 13% of courses participated, and the sample is heavily weighted toward upper-division courses, limiting representation of earlier stages in the undergraduate experience and our ability to assess developmental progression. So, while the results are positive, they are not yet comprehensive.
Across both outcomes, student performance is closely tied to assignment design. Where assignments are well aligned with GenEd outcomes, students demonstrate competency. Where that alignment is unclear—or where assignments do not explicitly ask for reflection, perspective-taking, or application—student performance drops accordingly.
So, what’s next?
* First, GEC recommends clearer and more explicit guidelines for aligning assignments with GenEd outcomes, particularly in Kuali submissions.
* Second, we recommend investment in faculty development—workshops and resources that help instructors design assignments that elicit the kinds of learning we are trying to measure.

* Third, and critically, we need to find a way to increase faculty participation in assessment. Without broader participation, we risk turning assessment into a compliance exercise rather than a meaningful tool for program improvement.
* Finally, we recommend that certain criteria be revisited—especially––and I emphasize this: language use within C2, to see how criteria are defined and implemented across disciplines, to ensure they are both rigorous and applicable.
A Key Emerging Concern: Language Proficiency
Among the most urgent findings echoed in both assessment data and anticipated student feedback, is the persistently low level of proficiency in a language other than English among our students. This isn't a marginal issue; it represents a structural weakness in the current GenEd framework.

At a time when we position global competency, intercultural awareness, and cross-cultural communication as central institutional goals, the fact that relatively few students graduate with functional proficiency in another language reveals a misalignment between our stated outcomes and our curricular realities. We're asking students to demonstrate global understanding without consistently providing them the most fundamental tool required to achieve it.
This raises a set of unavoidable questions for the committee and for the university: What is the role of language study within General Education? And more importantly, can we credibly claim to prepare students for global citizenship and an increasingly multilingual workforce if language proficiency remains peripheral to the curriculum?

Without sustained and meaningful engagement in language learning, our claims of intercultural competence risk remaining aspirational rather than demonstrable. If C2 is to function as more than a conceptual framework, then we need to treat language proficiency as a central pathway to achieving its goals, not as an optional enrichment. Despite our stated goals of fostering global understanding and communication across cultures, relatively few students graduate with functional proficiency in another language. This disconnect raises fundamental questions about:
* The role of language study within our GenEd requirements
* Whether GenEd is adequately preparing students for global citizenship and workforce demands
In short, the program is working, but unevenly. Students are learning, but not always in the ways we intend to measure. With stronger alignment, clearer expectations, and broader participation, we can close that gap.

Faculty Senate Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee Report #2001-02-1 November 19, 2001 As approved by the Faculty Senate on December 13, 2001 Amendments to the Constitution of the Faculty Senate Recent changes of titles and/or responsibilities of administration officials have affected certain ex officio members of the Faculty Senate listed in the membership paragraph (Article III) of the Faculty Senate Constitution. The Faculty Senate Executive Committee has asked the CBUM Committee to consider the constitution's membership article in light of these changes. At a meeting on November 7, 2001, the consensus of the CBUM Committee members was that no changes to the Senate Constitution are to be made without a referendum as provided for in Article VII of the Faculty Senate Constitution. That constitution, stating the Senate's fundamental principles, is too important a document to permit its being changed editorially; among other things because there may be disagreement on whether a change is editorial or substantive. This implies that changes to the titles and/or responsibilities of members of the administration who are also ex officio members of the Faculty Senate ought not to occur by administrative fiat, but are to be preceded by consultation with the body whose constitution they affect. Nevertheless, the CBUM Committee's consensus was that the following Senate Constitution changes required to make the document consistent with recent administrative action are comparatively non-controversial: From Vice Provost for Academic Programs and Services to Vice Provost for Academic Affairs. CBUM #1 http://www.uri.edu/facsen/CBUM 01-02-1.html 1 of 5 1/23/14, 1:59 PM

From Vice Provost for Research and Service to Vice Provost for Graduate Studies, Research and Outreach. From Vice President for Student Development to Vice President for Student Affairs. From Vice President for University Relations to Vice President for University Advancement. From Dean of Admissions and Financial Aid to Dean of Admissions. Accordingly, the CBUM Committee recommends that the Senate approve a future referendum authorizing those changes to the Senate Constitution. There are, however, also some changes that were deemed to be rather substantive. They are: The abolition of the Dean of the College of Continuing Education and concurrent institution of the position of Vice Provost for Urban Programs. The abolition of the Dean of the Graduate School and subsuming that official's responsibilities under those of the Vice Provost for Graduate Studies, Research and Outreach. The abolition of the position of Registrar and subsuming that official's responsibilities under the newly created position of Director of Enrollment Services. (Note that the Registrar, whose position is to be merged with that of another official who is as of now not even an ex officio member of the Senate, is a Faculty Senate Officer whose duties CBUM #1 http://www.uri.edu/facsen/CBUM 01-02-1.html 2 of 5 1/23/14, 1:59 PM

include an important function in conducting referendums.) Therefore, the CBUM Committee has decided to invite on the Senate floor an open discussion of these three substantive position changes, and to use the input of that discussion, possibly even including motions containing instructions to the committee, to frame recommendations with respect to future referendums on these matters.
It is hoped that the URI administration will, as a part of that discussion, provide its rationale and justification for the changes in administrative positions involved.
The committee also recommends that the constitutional amendments on the matters designated above as editorial be conducted only after the other matters have been disposed of in order that referendums possibly resulting from that disposition can be conducted simultaneously with the referendums recommended in this report.
In view of the above, the Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee recommends the following: 1.
That the five changes considered editorial by the Committee (see above) be included in a future referendum. 2.

That this referendum be postponed until the Faculty Senate has considered the matters designated above as substantive, and has made recommendations for referendums (if any) on these matters. 3.
That the Faculty Senate set aside time at this or a subsequent meeting to discuss the applicable University regulations and appropriate constitutional amendments resulting from these more substantive changes, including changes to clarify appropriate procedures and authority, and to authorize, if deemed appropriate, a referendum on these matters.
DISCUSSION POSTPONED DEFINITELY UNTIL JANUARY 24, 2002. 4.
That, in carrying out these referendums, the current Acting Registrar conduct the mail ballot required by Article VI of the Senate Constitution.

This summer at the request of President Carothers, the Board of Governors for Higher Education approved the change in title of the Vice President for Business and Finance to "Vice President for Administration.
Following is President Carothers' rationale for the title change from his memorandum on administrative reorganization: VPA http://www.uri.edu/facsen/VPA.html 1 of 4 1/23/14, 2:00 PM

The role of the vice president for business and finance has changed in recent years, with a much broader scope of responsibility evolving.
As we take on more enterprises, and as our partnerships with public and private companies and agencies grow, the vice president takes on more executive responsibility for managing these diverse activities.
In addition to the Alton Jones Campus, we now have both the Ryan Center and the Boss Arena as enterprise accounts, and within the timeframe of this plan we intend to establish a research corporation and explore seriously the establishment of a University sponsored retirement community.
More partnerships of the kind evolving with Amgen are likely, as the state anticipates our more aggressive involvement in building the economy of our state.
While the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs is the chief academic officer of the University and second to the President in the line of authority and responsibility, it is neither appropriate nor possible for her to take on these new areas.

Therefore it is my intent to rename the business vice president's position as the "Vice President for Administration," signifying the responsibility of this vice president for the overall management of the University, accountable to the Provost for support of the academic mission and to the President for everything else.
